title: Fox News Demands Unknown Callers Reveal Their Purpose Before Connecting
body:
When a call from an unfamiliar number lights up the screen, many users now have a new option: the phone can ask the stranger to state their name and purpose before the device actually rings. Apple’s iPhone, Google’s Pixel line and Samsung’s Galaxy series have all rolled out “call‑screening” features that place a brief, automated prompt in front of unknown callers, giving recipients a chance to decide whether to answer, mute, or send the call to voicemail.

The technology builds on existing voice‑assistant capabilities. On iPhones, the feature—dubbed “Silence Unknown Callers” with an added “Ask Caller to Identify Themselves” prompt—leverages Siri to greet the caller with a recorded message: “Please tell me who you are and why you’re calling.” Google’s Pixel uses its “Call Screening” tool, powered by Google Assistant, to not only request identification but also transcribe the response in real time, allowing the user to read the caller’s explanation while the phone remains silent. Samsung’s “Smart Call” operates similarly, using Bixby to request a brief introduction before connecting the call. In each case, the user can tap a button to accept the call, reject it, or let it proceed to voicemail, all without the phone’s ringtone ever sounding.

The rollout comes at a time when robocalls and spam calls have surged dramatically. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) estimates that more than 100 million unwanted calls are placed each day in the United States, many of which employ spoofed numbers to masquerade as legitimate businesses or contacts. Traditional call‑blocking apps have struggled to keep pace, often relying on blacklists that can be outdated or circumvented. By requiring unknown callers to speak before the call is connected, the new screening tools create a friction point that many automated systems cannot easily overcome, potentially reducing the volume of nuisance calls that reach consumers’ ears.

Industry analysts see the move as part of a broader shift toward AI‑driven user control in mobile communications. “We’re witnessing the convergence of voice assistants and telephony security,” says Maya Patel, senior analyst at TechInsights. “These features turn the phone into a gatekeeper, using natural language processing to filter out low‑effort spam while preserving the ability for genuine callers to get through.” However, Patel cautions that the effectiveness will depend on user adoption and the willingness of callers to comply. “If a legitimate business is unaware of the screening prompt, they might be dismissed as spam, which could frustrate both parties,” she adds.

Privacy advocates have raised questions about how the transcribed responses are stored and used. Google’s implementation, for instance, temporarily records the caller’s voice and generates a text transcript that appears on the screen, but the company asserts that the data is not retained beyond the call session. Apple’s approach is more conservative, offering the option to block the call without any recording. Samsung’s policy similarly emphasizes on‑device processing, limiting cloud exposure. Nonetheless, consumer groups urge manufacturers to provide clear disclosures and easy opt‑out mechanisms to prevent inadvertent data collection.

Early user feedback suggests mixed reactions. Some users appreciate the added layer of protection, reporting fewer interruptions from telemarketing firms that fail to pass the screening. Others find the extra step cumbersome, especially when receiving calls from unfamiliar but legitimate sources such as new clients, medical offices, or school administrators. To mitigate this, all three platforms allow users to whitelist certain numbers or contacts, ensuring that trusted callers bypass the prompt entirely.

Looking ahead, the adoption of call‑screening could influence regulatory standards and inspire further innovations in call authentication. The FCC’s STIR/SHAKEN framework, which authenticates caller IDs to combat spoofing, may eventually be paired with AI‑driven screening to create a multi‑tiered defense. As mobile operating systems continue to integrate sophisticated voice assistants, the line between user convenience and security is likely to blur, offering consumers more granular control over who gets through to their ears. Whether these tools will significantly curb the relentless tide of spam calls remains to be seen, but they mark a decisive step toward smarter, more proactive phone management.
